title: Pathology
tagline: Cell injury, inflammation, repair, haemodynamic disorders and neoplasia
summary: Pathology studies how disease changes cells and tissues. This course covers the general processes that underlie disease in every organ: cell injury and death, acute and chronic inflammation, healing and repair, oedema, thrombosis, embolism and shock, the biology and classification of cancer, environmental and nutritional disease, and the work of the pathologist.
overview: Pathology links the basic sciences to clinical medicine. It explains what injury does to cells, how the body responds, how repair can go wrong and what cancer is, and it provides many of the diagnoses on which treatment depends. This course teaches general pathology as a set of mechanisms, each tied to diseases that a doctor will meet, and then the practical work of the histopathologist and cytopathologist.

The first four chapters cover the basic responses of tissues. Cell injury explains adaptation, the boundary between reversible and irreversible injury, and the differences between necrosis and apoptosis. Acute inflammation follows the vascular and cellular events, the chemical mediators and the systemic acute-phase response. Chronic inflammation and repair covers macrophages, lymphocytes and granulomas, regeneration, scar formation and fibrosis. Haemodynamic disorders covers oedema and the Starling forces, congestion, haemostasis and thrombosis, embolism, infarction, disseminated intravascular coagulation and shock.

The next two chapters deal with neoplasia. The biology of cancer explains oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, DNA repair, the hallmarks of cancer, invasion and metastasis, and the chemical, physical and infectious causes of cancer. Diagnosing and classifying cancer covers benign and malignant tumours, nomenclature, grading and TNM staging, prognostic and predictive factors, tumour markers, screening and paraneoplastic syndromes. A chapter on environmental and nutritional disease covers tobacco, alcohol, drug injury, pollutants, radiation, undernutrition and obesity. The final chapter follows a specimen from biopsy to report, explains immunohistochemistry and molecular testing, shows how to read a cancer report, and describes the autopsy and the medical examiner system. Robbins and Cotran's textbook is the main reference throughout, with UK guidance where clinical practice is discussed.
outcomes: Describe the cellular adaptations to stress (hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy and metaplasia) and explain how dysplasia links them to cancer, with clinical examples.
Explain the mechanisms of reversible and irreversible cell injury, and distinguish necrosis from apoptosis by mechanism, appearance and consequence.
Describe the vascular and cellular events of acute inflammation, its main mediators and systemic effects, and interpret exudates, CRP and the white cell count.
Explain the cells and causes of chronic inflammation, the structure and differential diagnosis of granulomas, and the stages and complications of tissue repair.
Apply the Starling principle and Virchow's triad to explain oedema, thrombosis, embolism and infarction, and classify shock by mechanism.
Explain the multistep genetic basis of cancer, the roles of oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes and DNA repair, and how the hallmarks of cancer guide targeted treatment.
Name and classify tumours, distinguish grade from stage, and interpret tumour markers, screening results and paraneoplastic syndromes with their limitations.
Describe the pathology of tobacco, alcohol, drug toxicity, pollutants, radiation, undernutrition and obesity.
Follow a specimen from biopsy to report, and read a pathology report for diagnosis, grade, stage, margins, lymph nodes and predictive markers.

history.title: The seats and causes of diseases
history.detail: Giovanni Battista Morgagni, professor of anatomy at Padua, publishes De Sedibus et Causis Morborum, correlating the symptoms of about 700 patients with the findings at their autopsies. Disease is located in particular organs, the foundation of clinicopathological correlation.

history.title: Cellular pathology
history.detail: Rudolf Virchow publishes Die Cellularpathologie, arguing that disease is the disturbed life of cells and that every cell arises from another cell. The cell becomes the unit of pathology.

history.title: Leucocytes leave the blood
history.detail: Julius Cohnheim watches the living frog mesentery under the microscope and sees leucocytes adhere to the walls of small veins and pass through them, showing that pus cells come from the blood.

history.title: Phagocytes
history.detail: Élie Metchnikoff observes mobile cells in starfish larvae gathering around a thorn and proposes that inflammation brings phagocytic cells to defend the body. He shares the 1908 Nobel Prize with Paul Ehrlich.

history.title: Cancer from coal tar
history.detail: Katsusaburo Yamagiwa and Koichi Ichikawa produce skin cancers by repeatedly painting coal tar on rabbits' ears, the first experimental proof of chemical carcinogenesis.

history.title: Antibodies in tissue sections
history.detail: Albert Coons and colleagues label antibodies with a fluorescent dye and use them to locate antigens in tissue, the origin of immunohistochemistry, now used daily to determine the lineage of tumours and to measure predictive markers.

history.title: Two hits
history.detail: Alfred Knudson analyses the age at onset of retinoblastoma and proposes that the tumour requires two mutational events, one of which may be inherited. The idea explains tumour suppressor genes, and RB1 is cloned in 1986.

history.title: Apoptosis named
history.detail: John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie describe a controlled form of cell death with distinctive morphology and call it apoptosis.

history.title: The hallmarks of cancer
history.detail: Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg summarise cancer biology as six acquired capabilities, extended in 2011 and 2022. The framework organises research and the development of targeted treatments.

references.title: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
references.authors: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC (eds)
references.note: 10th edition. The standard reference for general and systemic pathology, and the main source for the mechanisms in this course.

references.title: Underwood's Pathology: A Clinical Approach
references.note: 7th edition. A UK textbook that links general pathology closely to clinical presentation.

references.title: Muir's Textbook of Pathology
references.note: 16th edition. A concise UK textbook of general and systematic pathology.

references.title: TNM Classification of Malignant Tumours
references.note: 9th edition, used for cancer staging in the UK from 1 January 2026.

references.title: WHO Classification of Tumours
references.authors: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board
references.note: 5th edition series (IARC), issued by organ system from 2019; the international standard for naming and classifying tumours.

references.title: Cancer datasets and tissue pathways
references.note: The UK standards for what a cancer pathology report must contain; updated continually, so check the current version of each dataset.
